indexEntry.name: Erie
indexEntry.mapNote: Approximate general area of the Erie, c.1600–1656: Erie and Chautauqua counties, New York, and Erie County, Pennsylvania (whole counties, not a boundary). Ohio is not drawn because the Erie’s western extent is contested. Low–medium confidence. The years 1654–1656 are the war and dispersal, not the years of settlement.
indexEntry.note: A general area on the south-eastern shore of Lake Erie (New York and Pennsylvania); nothing in Kentucky or Ohio.

territory.presenceNote: The Erie homeland was the south-eastern shore of Lake Erie (New York and Pennsylvania), outside Kentucky; nothing is drawn in Kentucky or Ohio. The area is shown c.1600–1656 (low–medium confidence): from the late 16th-century settlement of the Erie Plain to the dispersal. The years 1654–1656 in the story are the years of the war and dispersal, not of settlement. Where the Erie lived in Ohio is contested (the Oklahoma encyclopedia puts them as far as Toledo; archaeologists now place them in the east), so Ohio is not drawn.
territory.overlapNote: Seneca to the east; Neutral across the lake; Wenro north of the Buffalo River; the Whittlesey-tradition people, probably Algonquian, west of Presque Isle Bay. French maps drew the Erie along the whole south shore to Ohio; archaeologists now put them in the east (Wikipedia).
territory.basis: Archaeology and the Jesuit Relations (second-hand), via Wikipedia, the Encyclopedia of Cleveland History and the Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History. Wikipedia is a tertiary source.

eras.label: c.1600–1653 · South shore of Lake Erie
eras.text: The Erie, an Iroquoian people, lived along the south-eastern shore of Lake Erie between the Buffalo River and Presque Isle Bay, in palisaded maize villages. Seventeenth-century French maps put them east of a crescent-shaped lake that drains into Lake Erie, probably Chautauqua (Wikipedia; Encyclopedia of Cleveland History). The tint is three whole counties, an approximate general area, not a boundary. The c.1600 start is a round number for ‘late 16th century’; no source gives a year.
eras.apprTag: Approximate general area · Ohio not drawn (contested)

eras.label: 1654–1656 · War with the Seneca and Onondaga; dispersal
eras.text: In the summer of 1654, after a five-day flight inland, about 2,000 Erie warriors with their families made a stand in a palisaded fort and about 1,200 mostly Onondaga and Seneca warriors, many with Dutch muskets, took it (Jesuit Relation of 1655–56, via Wikipedia). Attacks went on, and by 1656 the Erie were slaughtered, dispersed or taken captive; captives were adopted by the Seneca and Onondaga. The fort site is not located. These are the war years, not the years they lived here: the tint is the same area as before. Afterwards a hypothesis links a remnant to the Richahecrians and the Westo of the Southeast, and sources date a surrender of survivors to the Seneca differently (1680 in the Oklahoma encyclopedia, 1682 in Wikipedia citing the Jesuit Relations). None of that is drawn.
eras.apprTag: Approximate general area · years of the war, not of settlement

territory.presenceLabel: Susquehannock or Conestoga village in this area
territory.presenceNote: This is a story about the eastern Beaver Wars, not a Kentucky village, and nothing is drawn in Ohio or Kentucky: no source consulted places the Susquehannock in the Ohio Valley. The homeland is the lower Susquehanna valley in Pennsylvania, shown c.1550–1763: the valley towns to 1675, the refuge in Maryland in 1675 (Prince George’s County), the last village in York County 1676–c.1680, then Conestoga Town in Lancaster County to 1763. Medium confidence for the counties; low–medium for the dates.
territory.overlapNote: Lenape (the Susquehannock held them tributary in the 1630s–40s; disputed), Piscataway in Maryland, Haudenosaunee, Occaneechi and Meherrin in Virginia (1676), and Seneca, Cayuga and Oneida who settled with the Conestoga. Some Susquehannock later became part of the Mingo (Wikipedia).
territory.basis: Archaeology (Kent 1984; the 1970 Pennsylvania excavation at the York County village) and colonial records, via Wikipedia and the Susquehanna National Heritage Area. Wikipedia is a tertiary source.

eras.label: c.1550–1675 · Lower Susquehanna valley
eras.text: From the mid-1500s the Susquehannock built palisaded towns in the lower Susquehanna valley, moving about every 25 years: Schultz (Lancaster County; at least 26 longhouses; its pottery type ends c.1600), Washington Boro (pottery type dated 1600–1635), then sites to c.1665 on the Lancaster County side; from c.1665 to 1675 the Upper Leibhart site on the west bank, York County (Wikipedia citing Kent 1984; Susquehanna National Heritage Area). Captain John Smith met Susquehannock representatives at the head of the Chesapeake in 1608. Earlier hamlets on the North Branch (Bradford County, Pennsylvania, and Tioga County, New York) and a short-lived settlement in Cumberland County are not drawn. The tint is two whole counties, approximate. The c.1550 start is a round number for ‘mid-1500s’.
eras.apprTag: Approximate general area · county tint medium, dates low–medium

eras.label: 1675 · Siege on Piscataway Creek, Maryland
eras.text: In 1675 the Susquehannock left the Susquehanna (the Susquehanna National Heritage Area says they were forcibly removed by the Seneca) and moved into Maryland, to a palisaded fort on Piscataway Creek, an abandoned Piscataway fort. In September 1675 about 1,000 Maryland and Virginia militia besieged them for about six weeks, and in early November they slipped away. Most crossed the Potomac into Virginia and camped on the Meherrin River near the Occaneechi; in January 1676 they raided the Rappahannock and James river settlements, which led to Bacon’s Rebellion (Wikipedia). The tint is Prince George’s County, Maryland; the Virginia camps are text only (the river is named, the counties are not).
eras.apprTag: Approximate general area · county tint medium, dates low–medium
eras.mapSubLabel: approximate general area · refuge and siege 1675

eras.label: 1676–c.1680 · Return to the valley (York County)
eras.text: Given leave to return in 1676, they built a last village on the hill now Native Lands County Park, York County: 16 longhouses and about 900 people (Susquehanna National Heritage Area, from the 1970 excavation). In 1677 the Haudenosaunee invited refugees to settle with them (Wikipedia); by 1680 the Haudenosaunee had forced them out, the village was empty, and its people had joined the Seneca, Cayuga and Oneida. The collapse ran over 1675–80 and was not one event.
eras.apprTag: Approximate general area · county tint medium, dates low–medium
eras.mapSubLabel: approximate general area · last valley village 1676–c.1680

eras.label: c.1685–1763 · Conestoga Town, Lancaster County
eras.text: In the late 1680s a group of Susquehannock and Seneca settled by the Conestoga River in Manor Township, Lancaster County, and became known as the Conestoga; Oneida and Cayuga families later joined them (Wikipedia). In 1700–01 William Penn took a deed to their lands and set aside a tract in Manor Township for them (Wikipedia; Pennsylvania Genealogy quotes the 1701 council). In December 1763 the Paxton Boys, a mob of settlers, murdered the last Conestoga in Lancaster County (Wikipedia). The Susquehannock as a distinct people are considered extinct from that date; descendants live among the Seneca–Cayuga Nation in Oklahoma and the Six Nations of the Grand River in Ontario. The point is the township, not the exact site.
